newsitem.title: CHINA: China firm unveils Internet business database.
newsitem.headline: China firm unveils Internet business database.

text.p: A Chinese joint venture on Saturday unveiled a state-supplied Internet database designed to bridge the geographical gap between foreign investors and customers and one million Chinese enterprises.

The Dragon Pulse business network would provide data supplied by China's State Council, or cabinet, to clients via the Internet global computer network, said officials of the service's creator Unicom-Sparkice.
"We are targeting the global Chinese community," said Edward Zeng, head of Unicom-Sparkice and of technology firm Sparkice, which holds a 49 percent stake in the venture.
China United Telecommunications Corp, an enterprise set up by 16 major organisations to compete with the Ministry of Posts and Telcommunications, holds the remaining 51 percent.

"By the year 2000, we will be the largest provider of Chinese global content," Zeng said in remarks to reporters at an opening ceremony for Unicom-Sparkice's third Internet cafe in Beijing, where staff unveiled the new database service.
Sparkice had bought three-year rights from the State Council to use data on one million Chinese companies compiled during a national census in 1995, company officials said.
"We now have information on one million companies," said company "media theorist", or spokesman, Steven Calcote.

A number of Chinese and joint venture companies have rushed to cash in on growing Internet-use in China and abroad by promising online business and financial services, although some have found it hard to aquire high-quality economic information.
While Sparkice would not check the accuracy of information supplied by the State Council or by companies themselves, it hoped firms would provide business references, Calcote said.
The venture hoped to expand Dragon Pulse services to include digital commerce, real-time financial data and government statistics releases, he said but gave no timescale.
Some of the information would be made available for free, but customers would be charged 48,000 yuan ($5,800) a year for full access in Chinese.

As well as the information provided by the State Council, Unicom-Sparkice hoped that many of the Chinese firms included in the database would sign up for further services, including advertising and custom-designed Internet addresses, he said.
So far, less than 100 companies had signed up for such services, which would cost 8,000-300,000 yuan a year, he said.
